# Resources, honestly annotated

Every list like this one tells you what a thing is good for. None prints the
one field that decides your evening. So here's the question this chapter
answers, once per entry, in the same words. What is this resource bad at?

## Four fields, and why the fourth is the one you need

An entry here says what the thing is, when you'd take it, what it costs, and
what it's bad at. The first three are on every resource page in this field. The
fourth is on none of them, because nobody advertises where their own material
stops working.

A resource doesn't fail in general. It fails you, at the point where what it
assumes about you and what's true about you come apart. A lesson that assumes a
working terminal is fine for the person who has one. You don't, so that
assumption is the first thing about it you need to read. Everything below is
free unless its entry says otherwise, and none of it wants an institutional
login.

## Why no address is printed next to any of these

None of the entries below carries a web address. A name outlives an address,
and it still finds the thing after a redesign that would have broken a printed
link.

The back of this book carries a dataset and source index. It holds every
address the book takes a number from, with the date that number was last
checked against the live page:

``` {.default .output}
https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P38398
9 facts, checked 2026-08-02
```

Nothing on this page is in that index, because this chapter takes no numbers
from anything below. The line at the end of the entries dates them instead.

::: {.check}
Find that UniProt line in the index at the back. It reads `9 facts, checked
2026-08-02`. Every line there has that shape: one address, one count, one date.
A date more than a year behind today makes what sits above it history.
:::

## Practice that marks your answer

**Rosalind** sets programming problems built on biology and marks what you
submit. Chapter 27 says when to take it and how far to go. The bad part: every
input it hands you is clean, so nothing there prepares you for a file like the
one in Chapter 15.

**The Galaxy Training Network** runs its tutorials on public Galaxy servers, in
a browser, with nothing installed, free and openly licensed. Use it to run a
whole analysis before you can write one. The bad part: a Galaxy history isn't a
script, so you finish holding nothing a stranger can re-run.

## The command line, which this book left out

**Software Carpentry's Unix Shell lesson** is the standard free route in, under
a Creative Commons license, and it's the one to take when you want the shell.
The bad part: before lesson one you download an archive and, on Windows,
install a shell to run it in.

**Happy Belly Bioinformatics**, by Mike Lee, is a working bioinformatician's
teaching site that starts at Unix and carries on into genomics. Nothing to pay.
The bad part: past the first pages it expects a Unix environment you set up and
tools you install yourself.

::: {.trap}
A page that loads is not a resource that's maintained. Tools change a default
more often than they remove the option. When that happens an old tutorial still
runs, warns about nothing, and hands you a number worked out a different way
from the one on the page. Look for a date and a version before you copy a
command off any page.
:::

## Reference for what you already use

**The Biopython Tutorial and Cookbook** documents the one library Chapter 17
installs, online and free, well past what that chapter needed. Open it when you
want a function you haven't met. The bad part: it tells you how to use `SeqIO`,
not whether `SeqIO` is what you want.

**EMBL-EBI's on-demand training** holds recorded webinars, self-paced tutorials
and course materials, free and openly licensed, from the institute that runs
Ensembl. Watch one to hear a database explained by the people who host it. The
bad part: a recording runs at the speaker's pace and never checks your work.

## The other half of the field, which is in R

**Bioconductor** is where a lot of published RNA-seq analysis happens, in R
rather than Python. Open source, free, one worked vignette per package. Go
there when the paper you're reproducing says DESeq2, because that's where
DESeq2 lives. The bad part: a vignette starts from data already in the shape
that package wants, and yours never arrives that way.

**Chatomics**, by Ming Tang, is a working bioinformatician's blog on R, Python
and single-cell data. The blog is free; the courses beside it aren't. Read a
post when it names your exact problem. The bad part: each post assumes whatever
setup he had open that day.

## Where a stranger will answer you

**Biostars** is the question-and-answer site Chapter 16 sent you to, free to
read. Bring it a question a search couldn't answer. The bad part: the standard
reply to "I have no lab" is to get one, and a badly formed question gets
silence rather than a correction.

**Bioinformatics Stack Exchange** is smaller and stricter than Biostars, and
free both to read and to post. Bring it a question with one right answer. The
bad part: anything without one gets closed instead of answered, so carry a
single failure and the exact text it printed.

## The two subjects this book stopped short of

**Automate the Boring Stuff with Python**, by Al Sweigart, is free to read
online under a Creative Commons license and assumes no programming at all. Take
it when Part 2 runs out and you want more Python. The bad part: there's no
biology in it anywhere.

**StatQuest**, by Josh Starmer, explains p-values, multiple testing and PCA in
short videos, free to watch. The study guides cost money. Start there if the
statistics in Chapter 25 went past you. The bad part: a video holds no data and
no code, so you can watch ten and still not have run one.

::: {.asof}
Every entry above was read on the live site on 2 August 2026, except Biostars
and Bioinformatics Stack Exchange, which refuse automated readers. Costs and
account rules move without notice, so check that field yourself before you
spend an evening on any of these.
:::

## Exercises

::: {.exercise num="30.1" time="30 minutes"}
::: {.goal}
Annotate one resource this chapter left out, and commit to the fourth field
before you open the thing.
:::
::: {.given}
Anything you can reach without paying and without an affiliation. A tool's own
documentation counts, and so does one person's blog.
:::
::: {.produce}
Five lines: your guess at the bad part first, then what it is, when you'd take
it, what it costs, and what it turned out to be bad at.
:::
::: {.check}
Compare your first line with your last. If they say the same thing, the bad
part was visible from the front page and you haven't been inside yet. Go one
level in and write it again.
:::

::: {.answerspace lines="6"}
:::
:::

## If it breaks

::: {.ifbreaks}
::: {.errfix err="404 Not Found"}
The site answered, so it's up and the address is what's gone. Search the site's
name plus the thing you wanted, instead of retyping what you have.
:::

::: {.errfix err="ERR_NAME_NOT_RESOLVED"}
Nothing answered at all. This is the fourth voice from Chapter 4, the network,
not the site. Open another page you know works. If that one fails too, the
trouble is between you and the internet.
:::

::: {.errfix err="A tutorial's command fails with an error the page never mentions"}
The page is older than the tool, so options got renamed under it. Read the
tool's own documentation for the option the error names, and treat the page as
a record of what somebody once did.
:::
:::

::: {.checkpoint}
- Name the four fields an honest annotation carries, and say which one gets
  left out everywhere else
- Say why no address is printed beside a resource on this page, and where the
  addresses this book does print are collected
- Pick the resource above that fits your next three hours, and say what it's
  bad at before you open it
- Write four fields for one resource nobody listed for you
:::

## Nobody sends the message

There's no message coming to tell you you're allowed. No acceptance, no first
day, nothing that marks the end of the beginner part. NCBI served you that
record in Chapter 5 without asking one question about who you are, and it'll
serve you another tomorrow morning. Go and ask it something nobody assigned
you.
